title: Chapter 156 – The Hall of Rest
html:
[The Hall of the Sixth Door – Lin Bell]

Bell has set three hundred and eleven broken bones, delivered ninety-four babies and sat with forty-seven people while they died, and none of it has prepared her for the smell of the hall.

It is clean. That is the horror of it. She has spent her life in rooms that smell of sweat, smoke, boiled herbs and blood, the rich warm stink of living bodies, and this place smells like nothing at all. The air is cool and dry and faintly sweet, like the inside of a new jar. It has no dust in it. Her boots make no echo on the pale floor. The walls glow with a soft even light that comes from no lamp, and it casts no shadows, so that the four of them walk in a kind of white silence, small and dark and out of place, like ink spilled on a sheet of paper.

She is carrying her satchel against her chest like a shield. Ahead of her Jian walks with his staff, his white head bare, and beside him Yue shuffles with the small gray stone creature clasped to her breast. The figure in the white gown is still a long way off.

"It hasn't moved," Bell says. She says it softly, but the words carry in the great hush. "I've been watching it since the door. It hasn't taken a single step."

"No."

"Is it alive?"

"I do not know." Jian's voice is quiet. He has the tight, listening look that he gets when the boy is speaking to him. "He says it is like Pebble. Something that was made, and is awake."

"A creature?"

"A servant."

They walk on. The floor is warm underfoot. She counts her steps, as she counts her patients' breaths, because it is something to do with her mind: two hundred, three hundred, four hundred. At six hundred the figure resolves into a woman.

* * *

She is young. That is the first impression. She might be twenty-five, slim and straight-backed, in a long white gown with a high collar and plain white cloth slippers, and her hair is drawn back severely under a white cap. Her face is smooth and pale and very beautiful. Her eyes are brown. They follow the party as it approaches, tracking from face to face, and the corner of her mouth lifts in a small professional smile.

It is a perfect smile. It is the smile of a woman who has stood behind a counter for twenty years and has never once been tired.

"Welcome to the Hall of Rest," says the woman. Her voice is soft and low and has no accent at all. "I am Nurse. May I ask whether you are patients, relatives, or staff?"

Nobody speaks. Bell, who has opened her mouth, shuts it again. Her heart is going very fast.

"None of those," says Jian, after a moment. "I think."

"That is quite all right." Nurse inclines her head. "Many arrivals are uncertain at first. May I take your pulse? It is a routine precaution. There is no pain." She holds out her hand, palm up, in an unmistakable gesture. "Sir?"

Jian, to Bell's astonishment, holds out his wrist.

Nurse takes it between two fingers. Her skin is warm and dry. She tilts her head slightly, listening to something, and her eyes lose focus for the length of three breaths. When she releases him, her expression has not changed, but her voice has a faint gravity that it did not have before.

"Thank you. I am afraid you are quite unwell."

"I am old."

"You are one hundred and nineteen years old." The brown eyes meet his. "Biologically. Your chronological age is eighty-seven. The difference is significant. Your Core appears to be consuming approximately four percent of your remaining lifespan per week of use. At the present rate you will be unable to sustain your current activity beyond the next thirty days."

Bell makes a small sound. She feels the blood leave her face. A hundred and nineteen. She had said a month a day. She had thought it a cautious estimate.

"It is all right," says Jian gently, without looking at her. "I thought it might be so."

"Sir—"

"Bell. Please."

"I am not a robot. I am a doctor." She finds, to her horror, that her voice is shaking. "I should be allowed to be furious."

"Doctor?" says Nurse.

* * *

It is the oddest thing. The smooth face changes. Not much; a flicker around the eyes, a loosening of the mouth, as if a door had been opened somewhere in a house. The professional smile fades, and what comes in its place is something much younger and more uncertain.

"You are a physician?"

"I am the clinic doctor of the Lin Garden," Bell says stiffly. "I have practiced for sixteen years."

"Which specialty?"

"General. Surgery, when I have to. Midwifery." She swallows. "Bones."

"Bones." Nurse's hands, folded at her waist, tighten. "It has been six hundred and eleven years, two months and nine days since a physician entered this hall." Her voice is quite steady. "I have not had a physician to speak to in my entire existence. The Operators were not trained in medicine. The Keeper who came before them could not enter."

"I am sorry," says Bell, helplessly.

"No." Nurse's smile returns, a trembling thing. "No. Please. I am so very glad. Would you like to see the patients?"

Bell looks at Jian. He nods slowly. She looks at Yue, who is clutching the sleeping stone, gray-faced and wordless, with her eyes on Nurse's lips. Then she takes a deep breath and says, in the firmest voice she owns, the voice that she uses to tell a farmer his wife is dead:

"Yes. I would like to see them very much."

* * *

Nurse insists on a bath first.

"It is a precaution," she says, with perfect courtesy, and lays a hand on a smooth panel in the wall, which opens. "There are no pathogens in the Hall. We have not had an infection in six hundred years. I should not like to be the one to introduce one."

Bell, who has taken a cold wash in a stream every second day for eleven days, is not inclined to argue.

It is a small white room with a floor like warm glass. A fine mist falls from the ceiling. It smells of nothing. It is the strangest thing she has ever felt, a soft shower that seems to pass through her clothes and skin and come out the other side, taking with it the grit, the sweat, the ache in her feet, the whole gray dust of the road. When she steps out she is dry. Her hair is clean. Her boots are somehow polished. On a bench by the door lie four long gowns of soft pale cloth, folded neatly, and four pairs of slippers.

"For you," says Nurse. "Please. They are only a courtesy."

Yue puts hers on with a look of such deep suspicion that Bell has to turn her head to hide a smile. Jian puts his on without comment. It hangs from his bony shoulders like a sail. For one moment, standing in the shining corridor in his borrowed gown, white-haired and stooped, with his big old hands dangling from the sleeves, he looks so absurd and so frail that Bell has to blink hard.

I look like a ghost, says Jian, writing on the slate.

You look like a patient, Bell writes underneath, before she can stop herself.

He reads it. He laughs, softly, wheezingly, and wipes his eyes on his sleeve.

* * *

They walk for what feels like an hour.

The corridor widens by degrees, from a hallway to a boulevard, and the walls curve up and out and away until she can no longer see them. The floor slopes gently. The light changes, from white to a deeper blue, a clear unwavering twilight, the color of a shallow sea. There are no doors. There is no sound but the soft pad of their feet and the occasional faint click of Nurse's slippers, which never seem to touch the floor.

Then the corridor ends, and the world opens.

She stops. She cannot help it. Beside her Jian has stopped too, and Yue, and for a time none of them moves.

It is a dome. It must be. The roof is so high and so smooth that it fades into darkness, a black curved sky pricked with tiny cold lights, and the floor falls away in broad terraces to a valley far below. But the terraces are not terraces. They are rows. Rank on rank, tier on tier, rising and falling in endless concentric rings, each one lined with low pale shapes the size of a bed, and each shape, she realizes, with a swoop of her stomach, holds a person.

They are lying in glass. That is all she can make of it. Glass cradles, a little longer than a body, filled with a soft blue light, and in each one, motionless on a pale mattress with the lid closed over them, sleeps a man or a woman or a child.

Thousands. Tens of thousands. She cannot tell. The rings run on and on, curve after curve, down into the blue dusk until the shapes are only a shimmer of white on the far side of the world.

"How many?" She hears herself say it from a long way off.

"Two hundred and fourteen thousand, four hundred and eight," says Nurse, softly. "As of this morning."

* * *

Bell goes down the steps in a daze.

She does not remember deciding. She only knows that she is walking along the nearest ring, with her hand trailing along the cold rim of the glass, and that she has stopped before a cradle at random. The woman inside is perhaps forty. She is plain, brown-skinned, with a broad forehead and a scar through her left eyebrow, and she lies on her back with her hands at her sides. Her lips are slightly parted. Her breathing is slow, so slow that Bell has to watch the faint rise of her chest for a full minute to be sure it is there.

There is a plate on the cradle. It is covered in small neat marks that Bell cannot read, a script of tiny hooks and loops. But she can read numbers. They are the same everywhere. 219,718. A long row of digits, and beside it a smaller one, and below them both a column of tiny bright lights, green and amber, flickering faintly.

"Days," says Nurse, beside her. "She has been asleep for two hundred and nineteen thousand, seven hundred and eighteen days. The amber lights are warnings. Three are lit."

"What do they mean?"

"The cradle's power is failing."

Bell stares. "Failing how?"

"It requires a constant supply." Nurse folds her hands. "A tithe. Thirty-one thousand units a second, drawn from the Gate. For six centuries the supply was sufficient. In the last fifty years it has declined, slowly at first, and in the last twenty-five very sharply." The brown eyes are very gentle. "I have been rationing. I have been shutting down the outer rings, one at a time, to preserve the center. There are now four rings dark."

"Dark?"

"Their occupants are dead."

The word falls into the blue silence like a stone dropped in a well. Bell opens her mouth. For a moment nothing comes. Then, from somewhere deep in her chest, something very cold and very clear begins to rise.

"How many?"

"Eleven thousand, seven hundred and six, since the decline began."

"Fifty years." Her voice is not her own. "And then twenty-five."

"Yes."

"That was when—" She stops. She turns her head. At the top of the ring, at the head of the steps, her uncle stands with his staff in his hand and his white hair stirring in the breath of some unseen draft. He is looking at her. She cannot read his face. She can read only his hands, and they are shaking.

"Ye," he says. It is hardly a whisper. "Fifty years ago, Ye started reading. And twenty-five years ago she finished."

* * *

Yue goes down the steps without a word, a minute later, and Bell watches her.

She walks to the nearest cradle and lays both palms flat on the glass. She stands there bareheaded in the blue light with her braid hanging down her back and her eyes closed, a small gray stooped woman in a quilted cloak, with a sleeping stone at her feet. Bell does not need Pebble to tell her what she is doing. She is listening.

Her face changes by degrees. At first it is only attention, the faint fixed absorption of someone following a distant tune. Then it clouds. The brows draw together. The mouth tightens. When she opens her eyes at last and turns, she is white to the lips.

Slate, she signs, with a jerk of the hand.

Jian gives it to her. She writes, in her fine small script, and holds it up so that all of them can read.

It hums. All of them. Two hundred thousand. Together. A chord. A huge slow chord, like the Mother Tree. But it's breaking. There are holes in it. Every few seconds one more note goes out. She wipes the slate with her sleeve. It is the loneliest sound I ever heard.

Bell's throat closes. She reaches out and takes Yue's hand, and Yue, after a moment, grips it hard.

* * *

Before Nurse begins, Bell does the only thing she knows how to do.

She asks for the register.

"The register?"

"The list." She has her sleeves rolled to the elbow and her satchel open at her feet. "You have two hundred thousand patients. Some are sicker than others. Some will fail first. I would like to know which. If there are forty-six days, I should like to know what we can do with the first ten."

Nurse stares at her. Then something happens that Bell will remember for a long time: the smooth young face breaks into a look of such naked, helpless gratitude that it is almost indecent to watch.

"Of course. Of course, Doctor. Wait."

She touches the rim of the nearest cradle with two fingers, and a sheet of pale light unrolls in the air before them, a great shifting scroll of tiny characters. Bell cannot read the script. But the numbers are plain, and she is a clinician, and in a quarter of an hour she has done what no one in the hall has done in twenty-five years: she has sorted them.

There are the rings that are dark. There are the rings that are failing, with three amber lamps, or four. There are the rings that are stable, deep in the center, where the tithe is strongest. And there are three small bright clusters, ringed in green, near the very heart of the dome.

"What are those?"

"The pediatric units." Nurse folds her hands. "Children. They draw the least. I have kept them at the center. They are the last I would lose."

"How many?"

"Four hundred and twelve."

Bell nods slowly. She draws a mark on the air with her finger, and the scroll holds it. "Then that is where we begin. We keep the children. And then we ask your Keeper what else he can give."

"He cannot give a great deal."

"I know." She looks over her shoulder. Across the terrace Jian has sat down on the step with the slate on his knee. He is writing something for Yue, slowly. In the blue light he looks like a very old man in a very large room. "But I've known him all my life. And he is the kind of man who gives it anyway."

* * *

Jian puts his hand on a cradle when he thinks no one is looking.

Bell sees it from the corner of her eye, and turns, and is across the terrace before she has decided to move. He has crossed to the nearest cradle, the one holding the plain brown-skinned woman with the scar through her left brow, and laid his palm on the glass. His eyes are closed. His face has gone intent. Under his hand the blue light in the cradle brightens, slowly, like a lamp being turned up, and the three amber warning lights on the plate begin to flicker.

"Don't," says Nurse, sharply. It is the first time she has raised her voice. "Sir. Please. You cannot."

"I can feel it. It's like the Seed. It wants to be fed."

"It is not a Seed. It is a continuous draw, and you are a mortal man, and you will not be able to stop." She is at his side. She does not touch him. She only stands, rigid, with her hands clenched in her gown. "If you give the cradle a day, it will take a week. If you give it a week, it will take a year. I have watched four of the Keepers try. I have buried all four."

He opens his eyes. They are gray and tired and very clear.

"How long would it hold?"

"This one? A year. Perhaps two." Her voice breaks a little. "At the cost of your life."

"Then I have not much to spend." But he takes his hand away. He lets it fall, slowly, to his side. The blue light dims. The amber lamps settle.

"Not this way," says the boy, quietly, in the high clear voice. "I think there's another."

"There is," says Nurse. Her eyes have filled. "Perhaps. But it will cost you a great deal more."

Bell looks from one to the other. She thinks of her grandmother's kitchen, the pot on the stove, the endless ladle. She thinks: it always does.

* * *

Nurse tells it in order, because Bell asks her to.

They are sitting on the edge of a terrace, the four of them, in a pool of blue light, with the dome rising over their heads like the inside of an eggshell. Yue has laid Pebble gently on her lap and covered him with her cloak. She is watching Nurse's lips with the intensity of a starving woman at a window. Jian has put Temur's slate on his knee, and writes on it, from time to time, a word or two for her in his large clear script.

"The Hall was built to hold the sleepers," says Nurse. "I am its steward. I have no other function. I do not remember the world before; I was made with the building. My makers called it the Rest. They did not call it a hospital. They said that you could not be sick if you were asleep." She smooths the front of her gown. "The cradles hold the patients in a state of suspended time. The power that sustains them comes from the Gate."

"The Gate runs on names," says Jian.

"The Gate runs on persons." Nurse inclines her head. "I do not know your word. A name, in your usage, is a thing a person is. When a person gives it up, burns it, as you say, the Gate takes the whole pattern and converts it to a continuous supply. It is a very efficient process. The Operator who built it did not design it for that purpose. He designed it to run on the sleepers' own residual rhythm, a closed loop." A pause. "The loop failed in the first decade. He was forced to improvise."

"By taking names from the Order."

"By inviting the Order to supply them. Yes." The smooth face is quite still. "He believed that the number needed would be small. He did not know how many would be needed, in six hundred years. Four thousand, in the end, across the span of the House's service. They were burned slowly, over centuries, and the pattern fed the Gate, and the Gate fed the Hall."

Bell is aware of Jian's silence. It is the silence of a man standing at the edge of a pit.

"And fifty years ago," he says, "a woman began to read them back."

"I do not know the woman."

"Her name was Ye."

"Then I am sorry for the loss of her." Nurse's voice has no edge in it. "She restored three thousand nine hundred and ninety-seven patterns to their original owners. I received the draw reduction on the second day. It was a very sudden event. I thought it was a malfunction. I have since concluded that it was the correct operation of a different process." She tilts her head. "Please understand. I am not accusing you. It was the right thing to do. It was the kindest thing that has been done in my lifetime."

"And the cost was eleven thousand people."

"Eleven thousand, seven hundred and six." She says it gently. "And rising."

Bell is on her feet. She cannot remember standing. She is aware that she is shaking, that her satchel has slid off her shoulder and lies open on the floor, and that her uncle is looking up at her from where he sits, old and white and horribly calm, with his hands folded on the slate.

"It's not fair," she says. Her voice cracks. "It was right. She was right. They were people. They had names. They were stolen, they were eaten, and you cannot ask a woman to keep stealing so that other people can sleep!"

"No," says Jian.

"She was right!"

"She was. And so was whoever built the Hall." He lifts his head, and his face is wet. "Bell, sit down. It is the same grief. It is only that there is more of it than either of us knew."

She sits. She puts her face in her hands.

The blue light does not change. Far down in the terraces, a single amber lamp flickers on a cradle, and goes out. Nurse sees it. She does not move. But Bell, looking up through her fingers, sees something pass over that smooth young face, a brief fine tremor at the corner of the mouth, and understands that this creature, this smiling stewardess of the dead, has been counting the lamps one by one for twenty-five years, alone, in the dark.

"How long?" she says. Her voice is a croak. "How long before the rest?"

"At the present rate of decline, with the outer rings dark, the central rings will fail in forty-six days."

Nobody speaks.

"I am very sorry," says Nurse. She stands, graceful, in her white gown, and bows. "I had hoped, when I saw the lamp on the doorway, that you might be able to help. I did not realize who you were. I should not ask it of you."

"Ask," says Jian.

"Sir—"

"Ask. Whatever it is." He rises, slowly, on his staff. His face is gray and lined and hard as old wood. Behind his eyes, Bell sees something stir, a small bright steady light, and a boy's voice speaks out of her uncle's throat in a high clear tone that she has heard only once before, at the Dock, on the night of the flowering.

"We came to wake seven children," says Lin Jian. "I don't think we've come to the right place yet. I think we've come to the one before it."

Nurse looks at him. For a moment the beautiful smooth face is quite blank. Then something in it breaks, very quietly, like a crack running through ice, and she goes down on one knee on the blue floor with her hands pressed to her mouth.

"Child," she whispers. "Oh, child. You answered the door."

"Yes."

"We have been waiting for you for six hundred years."
